chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Fletcher's open ninth harmonies and classical passages
summary: Fletcher spread ninth chords, experimented to sound different, and inserted classical passages such as Humoresque into standard tunes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Did he like to search out when he was at the keyboard? Did he like to search out -- you know, you used the term pretty chords. Do you consider him to have been an innovator with regard to harmony?

Yes, he was more or less bent on playing the open harmony, you know, like the nin-ths -- he would spread them out instead of having them closed sometimes, you know, and he always would experiment. He was always searching, you know, looking for something that would sound different because of the vast amount of arrangements he had to do, but even if he had spare time on his hands, he would still play the piano. And of course, I tell you a lot of things he would do, and, Tom, he would insert a lot of classical passages, you know, in his -- even in his playing
piano in extended the standard tunes, you know.

And as you know, some of the best riffs are the classical things, you know, I know Coleman Hawkins used to (unintelligible) could play a lot of those funny things, you know. And getting back, staying with Fletcher for a minute, he'd play on the piano and he'd -- things like "Humoresque" and all those things. He would spread his chords out and one of those all these things. I know he'd get up and get a drink of water sometimes. He'd stand on the floor and look at the space, and you could tell he was thinking of things. Then he'd go back and then he'd play it a little different, you know, and I think his reason for that is because of the fact that he was trying to make a decision in his mind which pattern should he use, you know.
